title: The wick drawn down
hook: Patacara watches the lamp's wick pulled down and the flame go out, and is free (Therigatha, Patacara)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uttama, who left her dwelling four, five times, until she sat. Your line was she stayed. Did you stay one minute longer with something? Today, the teacher she went to. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

Night. A small hut. A clay lamp burning beside a bed. A woman sits down on the bed and takes up a needle. She reaches into the lamp, draws the wick down, and the flame goes out. In the Therigatha, that is the moment Patacara's mind comes free. The path met her before, as the woman who lost everything and became a teacher of grieving women. The commentary says she taught Uttama too. Today, Patacara's own poem, and the lamp at the center of it.
screen: `A HUT AT NIGHT.` → `A NEEDLE AND A LAMP.` → `THE FLAME GOES OUT.`

segments.voice: First, her question. The poem opens in the fields. Men plow with their plows and sow seed in the ground, and they gain wealth and support their wives and children. Then Patacara asks: I keep the precepts, I do what the Teacher taught, I'm not lazy and I'm not proud. Why haven't I come free? It's an honest complaint, and the poem keeps it. Second, the water. She washes her feet, the poem says, and watches the water run down the slope. She steadies her mind, the way a good horse is trained. The path will come back to that washing tomorrow. Third, the lamp. Then she takes a lamp and goes into her dwelling. She looks over the bed, sits down on it, takes a needle, and draws down the wick. Fourth, the word. Like the going out of the lamp, the poem says, was the release of her mind. And the Pali uses a very particular word for the lamp going out: nibbana. The same word the tradition uses for the goal of the whole path. In this poem it's not abstract at all. It's a flame in a clay lamp, and a woman with a needle, watching it go. No one blows it out. The wick is drawn down, and the flame has nothing left to hold onto. So the flame goes out. The poem doesn't explain the image. It sets the small, ordinary act of putting a lamp out for the night beside the freedom the whole path aims at, and lets them sit together.
screen: `WHY NOT ME?` · `WATER RUNNING DOWN THE SLOPE.` · `A NEEDLE DRAWS THE WICK DOWN.` · `NIBBANA: THE LAMP GOES OUT.` · then, large: `THE FLAME GOES OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a flame go out. If a candle is nearby and it's safe, light it, watch it for a few breaths, and then put it out and watch the last of the smoke rise. If not, dim a lamp or a screen, or close your eyes and wait for one thought to end on its own, the way a flame ends when nothing feeds it. Don't push the thought away. Just watch it finish. Then rest in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Nibbana. The going out of a lamp's flame, the very word Patacara's poem uses as her mind comes free while she draws down the wick. Today's word.
Your line: the flame goes out. Tonight, when you switch off the last light, pause in the dark for one breath before you move. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the image of a lamp going out when explaining nibbana, and in Theravada communities Patacara's verse is read as a picture of it, told by a woman who had known great loss.

fork.setup: Patacara has washed her feet and watched the water run down the slope. now she takes a lamp into her dwelling and sits on the bed. what does she do with the lamp?
options: reads by it late into the night.
takes a needle and draws down the wick.
carries it out to the other nuns.
fork.reveal: she sits, takes a needle and draws down the wick. as the flame goes out, her mind comes free.

original.note: Pali nibbāna (Sanskrit nirvāṇa): the going out of a flame; the word the tradition uses for the goal of the path.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman blowing out a candle.
what it means: a lamp's quiet going out is the picture of her freedom.
what a scholar hears: the Pali uses the same word, nibbana, for the lamp going out and for the mind's release: like the nibbana of the lamp.

sources.ref: Therigatha commentary on Uttama (Patacara as her teacher)

notes: Thig 5.10 paraphrased in order: plowmen and wealth; her question (virtuous, doing the Teacher's bidding, not lazy or proud, why no release?); washing her feet and watching water flow down the slope; steadying the mind like a thoroughbred horse; taking a lamp into her dwelling, looking at the bed, sitting, drawing the wick down with a needle; 'like the nibbana of the lamp was the release of mind'. Confirm all details.
The poem's use of nibbana for the lamp (padipass' eva nibbanam) is stated as in the text; confirm the Pali.
'Nobody blows it out ... the fuel is drawn away' is the writer's explanation of the image; confirm it is fair across schools.
Foot-washing is mentioned in one sentence only; tomorrow (787) teaches the thirty nuns' foot-washing.
howItsDone: 'often' and 'one of the clearest pictures' are soft claims; confirm or soften further.

Editor pass: 'the fuel is drawn away' and 'nothing is destroyed' (interpretation beyond the verse) trimmed to the wick drawn down; superlative 'deepest freedom the tradition names' removed; 'lower a lamp' to 'dim a lamp'.
